# Preface

For the final exam/project we will develop classification models using several approaches and compare their performance on a new dataset that is a subset of one of the datasets used in machine learning common task framework (CTF) competitions.  A copy of it split into training (`final-data-train.csv`, with outcome `response` available) and test (`final-data-test.csv`, stripped of the outcome, for prediction purposes only) datasets is available on our course website in Canvas as a zip-archive of all associated files.

Please notice, that at the end of this final exam/project you will be asked, in addition to the Rmarkdown and HTML files, to also make predictions for the observations in the *test* (not training!) dataset and upload them into Canvas as well.  The expected format for the file with predictions for test dataset is two columns of comma-separated values, one row per observation in *test* dataset, first column -- the observation identifier (column `id` in test dataset) and the second column -- your best model predictions for each observation in the *test* dataset as Y/N indicator.  To illustrate expected format the zip archive contains also a couple of examples of test predictions in this format for your reference as well (`predictions-*.csv` files in `predictions-examples` sub-folder in zip-archive).

One more time, to iterate and emphasize, please notice that this time your submission must consist of the following *three* (not just two, Rmd+html, as usual) items:

* Rmarkdown *.Rmd file with all the calculations you want to receive credit for,
* HTML version of the output generated by your *.Rmd file, and
* **predictions** for the **test** dataset in comma-separated values (CSV) format (file name **must** have *.csv extension for the file to load in Canvas)

The teaching team invites you to load your predictions (just predictions, just for the test dataset according to the file format shown in the sample files in the zip-archive) into Canvas repeatedly as you work on your models and improve them over the course of this week.  At least daily (or more frequently as we see fit) we will download predictions loaded by everyone by that time and compile a leaderboard in html format of all of them sorted by their accuracy as compared to the true values of the outcome for the test dataset (along with their sensitivity, specificity, etc.).  This list will be made available on our course website in Canvas for everyone in this class in order to see how the performance of their models compares across the rest of the models built by other students in the class.  The first version of the leaderboard posted on the course website at the time when final exam is made available starts with predictions made by those few example files provided in the zip-archive (coin flip, majority vote, etc. -- what do you think Charlie Brown is using to make the predictions?).  Those should be pretty easy to improve upon.

It is 100% up to you whether you want to upload your model predictions over the course of this week, how frequently you want to do it and what you want its results to be called in the leaderboard posted for everyone in the class to see.  We will use the name of the 2nd column in the file with predictions (the one containing Y/N values, not the numerical ids of the observations) as the model name listed in the leaderboard.  If you prefer not to use your name, choose something else instead, sufficiently unique so that it is easier for you to spot your result among all others.  Once again, please check out sample files of dull (majority vote, coin flip, etc.) predictions we have made available and consider how they show up in the leaderboard html file already posted on Canvas website.  Once you are done with final you are expected to load predictions from your best model into Canvas -- that is part of your points total as explained below.

Lastly, the size of this dataset can make some of the modeling techniques run slower than what we were typically encountering in this class.  You may find it helpful to do some of the exploration and model tuning on multiple random samples of smaller size as you decide on useful ranges of parameters/modeling choices, and then only perform a final run of fully debugged and working code on the full dataset.  Please see also the afterword below on the computational demands of this problem set.

# Problem 1: univariate and unsupervised analysis (20 points)

Download and read training and test data into R and prepare graphical and numerical summaries of it: e.g. histograms of continuous attributes, contingency tables of categorical variables, scatterplots of continuous attributes with some of the categorical variables indicated by color/symbol shape, etc.  Whatever you find helpful to think about properties of the data you are about to start using for fitting classification models.

As it is often the case for such contests, the attributes in the dataset are blinded in the sense that no information is available about what those are or what their values mean.  The only information available is that the attribute `response` is the outcome to be modeled and the attribute `id` is the unique numerical identifier for each observation.  Some of the remaining attributes are clearly categorical (those that are character valued) and some rather obviously continuous (those with numerical values with large number of unique values).  For several of them it is less clear whether it is best to treat them as continuous or categorical -- e.g. their values are numerical but there are relatively few unique values with many observations taking the same value, so that they arguably could be treated as continuous or categorical. Please identify them, reflect on how you prefer to handle them and describe this in your own words.

Perform principal components analysis of this data (do you need to scale it prior to that? how would you represent multilevel categorical attributes to be used as inputs for PCA?) and plot observations in the space of the first few principal components indicating levels of some of the categorical attributes of your choosing by the color/shape of the symbol.  Perform univariate assessment of associations between the outcome we will be modeling and each of the attributes (e.g. t-test or logistic regression for continuous attributes, contingency tables/Fisher exact test/$\chi^2$ test for categorical attributes).  Summarize your observations from these assessments: does it appear that there are predictors associated with the outcome `response` univariately? Which predictors seem to be more/less relevant?

Answer: First, Charlie Brown was probably also using a coin flip or some kind of other random number generator that yields 50/50 divisions for probability (e.g., rolling a die and comparing probability of rolling a 1,2 or 3 vs. probability of rolling a 4,5, or 6).

I followed all of the steps to conduct univariate, bivariate and unsupervised analysis of these data. First, I loaded the entire dataset (i.e., training dataset) into R as a data.frame, and then converted the "id" column to be the rownames in the dataset. Second, I summarized the dataset to examine the mean, median, standard deviation and range of all variables, as well as to calculate the number of missing (i.e., NA) values. There are n = 30,994 observations and 18 variables (1 outcome variable and 17 input features) in the dataset with no missing values and all of the variables are relatively normally distributed, with no skew values greater than 3 or less than -3. The 6 continuous variables have a limited range (max range = 17) and limited variation, with the exception of the variable "ypz", which has a standard deviation of 5.48 (M = 6.38). 

Examining the frequency tables of categorical attributes, there are more "N" values for the response variable than "Y" values, and the 3 other binary variables have similar, somewhat unbalanced distributions (i.e., considerably more of 1 category than the other category). The additional 8 categorical variables have considerable variation, yet some response categories are very rare (e.g., for "bnf", there are only 8 cases with "O", or for "zwp", there are only 21 with "z"). To allow analyses to proceed, all categorical features will later be converted to separate dummy variables for each category and the original categorical variables will be removed from the dataset.

The histograms generally confirm the findings from the descriptive statistics, yet also show that "djt" and "is" might have skewness and some non-normality. Boxplots also support the results from the descriptive statistics above by showing that "ypz" has considerable variability, and also reveal that "qh" and "is" have a handful of potential outliers near the maximum values for these variables.

I chose to model all variables that take on numerical values as continuous (and non-numeric variables as factors), because even if a variable is ordinal, it can act as a pseudo-continuous variables in analyses. Furthermore, modeling these variables this this way would take up fewer degrees of freedom and reduce the number of parameters to be estimated if I had instead recoded these limited category numeric variables as k - 1 dummy variables or one-hot encoded dummy variables.

Turning to the bivariate analyses in the correlation matrices and pairs panels with coloring for the response variable, these results show that most of the input features are significantly associated with the outcome variable, yet this is not unexpected given the very large sample size and high statistical power. The pairs panels reveal that the continuous attributes are all significantly related to the outcome variable and these relationships are positive, ranging from RHO = 0.08 to RHO = 0.30. Because correlations might not fully model all relationships, it is also important to examine other measures of association, including t-tests for continuous attributes and Fisher's exact tests for categorical attributes.

The results from the t-tests show that all continuous variables have significantly different means for cases with response = N and response = Y, which is likely due to the large sample size (and high statistical power), because the actual absolute value of the difference in means is small for all of these variables. However, due to these relationships and their significant correlations above, these variables should be retained as predictors in the models.

The results from the Fisher's exact tests (with Monte Carlo simulated p-values due to the large dataset and computing time for non-parametric exact tests more generally) show that each categorical feature is also significantly related to the outcome variable, as shown by very small p-values, which again, is due to the very large sample. However, because Fisher's tests do not yield an effect size for larger than 2 X 2 tables, the magnitude of these relationships is not clear and correlation coefficients for the dummy coded categorical variables are more suitable to assess the strength of relationships.

Moving to the PCA, in which I first created dummy variables for all categorical attributes and scaled all attributes to mean = 0 and SD = 1, these results reveal that the first two principal components explain about 10% of the variance in the dataset. The four separate biplots of the first two principal components with colored points for the response variable, as well as the variables "wc", "bnf" and "ent" reveal some interesting findings about the data. Specifically, there appears to be a clear separation of the "response" and "wc" variables along the principal components eigenvector, whereas the "bnf" and "ent" variables have a less defined separation, and therefore, might be less helpful in their explanatory ability as input features.

Overall, due to the relatively high dimensional dataset and the limited predictive ability of input features that are not predictive of the outcome, I decided to subset this dataset into relevant features only by including only features with an absolute value of their Spearman correlation of 0.05 or greater. This approach to dimension reduction successfully removes less relevant features (i.e., "noise" variables) and only retains the ones (i.e., "signal" variables) that will help inform the prediction of the outcome variable. 

Note: For the more computationally-intensive models, I also randomly sampled from the dataset based on the specific guidance in the Preface and Afterword of this Final Exam to reduce the overall number of observations, so that this file would knit in a reasonable period of time. I experimented with using all observations, but the file took several hours to knit. I could have run these same models with the full dataset, but without a multi-core machine with parallel processing or a cloud platform such as AWS, Google Cloud Platform or Microsoft Azure, the time to knit for me and the Teaching Fellows would be prohibitive.

```{r Problem 1 Univariate and Unsupervised Analysis, width = 10}
#reading in .csv training dataset

#checking spearman correlations for all variables
rcorr(as.matrix(train1dums_num[,c(1:15)]), type = "spearman")

rcorr(as.matrix(train1dums_num[,c(1,31:ncol(train1dums_num))]), type = "spearman")

#scatterplot pairs panels with
#response variable colored by class (Y and N)
#running pairs panels (the full dataset took >60 minutes for

ggpairs(train1dums_num[,c(1:7)], aes(colour=factor(response)), 
        progress = TRUE, upper = list(continuous = wrap("cor", size = 3)))


#t-tests for outcome variable and continuous attributes

ttest_res1 <- as.data.frame(t(sapply(train1[,c(5,7,9:11,18)], function(x) unlist(t.test(x ~ train1$response,
                                                 conf.int = TRUE,

                                                 conf.int = TRUE,

pca1$rotation[,1:20]

biplot(pca1, pc.biplot=T, cex = 0.6)

autoplot(pca1, data = train1, colour = 'response',

#calculating features that are most

train1dums <- train1dums_num[,c(names(train1_corrs2))]
```

# Problem 2: logistic regression (20 points)

Develop logistic regression model of the outcome `response` as a function of multiple predictors in the model.  Which variables are significantly associated with the outcome?  Test model performance on multiple splits of data into training and test subsets and summarize it in terms of accuracy/error/sensitivity/specificity.

Answer: I fit binary logistic regression models with all relevant input features from above with k-fold validation and 25 training and testing splits to calculate accuracy (1-accuracy = misclassification error), sensitivity (i.e., true positive rate), and specificity (i.e., true negative rate) for each subset from the resampling procedure. These results show that all input features significantly predicted the outcome variable, except for "bw", "tdt_sm" and "sb_s7". 

This means that the odds ratio for each of these significant variables is significantly different from 0, suggesting that they have an association of some degree of magnitude with the binary outcome variable, "response." In fact, the odds ratios are quite high in magnitude in some instances, with 7 of the odds ratios greater than 10. The accuracy and specificity were relatively high for these models, yet they also yielded a somewhat high false negative rate, as shown by the sensitivity values nearing a 70% true positive rate. 

My plots below for Problem 6 show the logistic regression results alongside all other types of models (including box plots of accuracy for each modeling approach), to provide context for the model performance of the logistic regression model as compared to the other modeling approaches' model performance.

```{r Problem 2 Logistic Regression, warning=FALSE}
#estimating binary logistic regression model
#predicting response as outcome
lreg1 <- glm(response ~ ., family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = train1dums)

#printing model and calculating odds ratios 
#and confidence intervals
summary(lreg1)
exp(lreg1$coefficients)
exp(confint(lreg1))

#creating helper function to calculate model
#performance metrics
assess.prediction <- function(truth,predicted) { 
predicted <- predicted[ ! is.na(truth) ] 
truth <- truth[ ! is.na(truth) ]
truth <- truth[ ! is.na(predicted) ] 
predicted <- predicted[ ! is.na(predicted) ] 
# overall accuracy of the test: how many cases # (both positive and
# negative) we got right:
accuracy <- signif(sum(truth==predicted)*100/ length(truth),3)
TP <- sum(truth==1 & predicted==1) 
TN <- sum(truth==0 & predicted==0) 
FP <- sum(truth==0 & 
predicted==1) 
FN <- sum(truth==1 & predicted==0)
P <- TP+FN
N <- FP+TN
sensitivity <- signif(100*TP/P,3)
specificity <- signif(100*TN/N,3)

return(res1 <- rbind(accuracy,sensitivity,specificity))
}

#conducting 25-fold cross validation to calculate
#model performance for logistic regression model
data <- train1dums
nTries <- 25
lregtrainres1 <- list()
lregtestres1 <- list()
for ( iTry in 1:nTries ) {
  bTrain <- as.numeric(sample(rownames(data),size=nrow(data)*0.8))
    rsTrain <- glm(response~.,family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = data[bTrain,])
      # make and assess predictions in training dataset:
      lregtrain1 <- assess.prediction(data[bTrain,c("response")], ifelse(predict(rsTrain, newdata = data[bTrain,],type = "response") > 0.5,1,0))
      #fit model in test dataset
      rsTest <- glm(response~.,family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = data[-bTrain,])
      # make and assess predictions in test dataset:
      lregtest1 <- assess.prediction(data[-bTrain,c("response")], ifelse(predict(rsTest, newdata = data[-bTrain,], type = "response") > 0.5,1,0))
      #saving results to two separate lists
      lregtrainres1[[iTry]] <- lregtrain1
      lregtestres1[[iTry]] <- lregtest1
  }

#printing results for logistic regression models
#training dataset error
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(lregtrainres1, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(lregtrainres1, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(lregtrainres1, "[[",3))
#all results
lregtrainres1

#test dataset error
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(lregtestres1, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(lregtestres1, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(lregtestres1, "[[",3))
#all results
lregtestres1


```

## Extra points problem: interaction terms (5 extra points)

Assess the impact/significance of pairwise interaction terms for all pairwise combinations of covariates used in the model and report the top ten that most significantly improve model fit.

Answer: For this problem, I first created a function to create a new dataset with all pairwise combinations of covariates used in the model as multiplicative interaction terms, resulting in a new dataset with 465 variables. 

I fit binary logistic regression models with relevant input features with k-fold validation and 25 training and testing splits to calculate accuracy (1-accuracy = misclassification error ), sensitivity, and specificity for each subset from the resampling procedure. Due to the number of features (465), the model encountered separation and convergence issues, so I experimented with fewer input features, and 100 features allowed the model to successfully converge. 

These results show that adding these interaction terms did improve sensitivity considerably (i.e., a ~6% increase in both the training and test dataset), yet accuracy and specificity stayed relevantly similar to the logistic regression model with no interaction terms. These findings suggest that interaction terms, which allow for modeling more complex and nonlinear variable relationships, can increase model performance (by decreasing bias at the expense of variance) and enhance prediction in both the training and testing dataset, without causing the model to overfit.

```{r Extra Points Problem Interaction Terms, warning=FALSE}
#creating new dataset with pairwise interaction
#terms for all pairwise combinations of covariates
#used in model above

#subsetting predictor variables only
train1dumsxonly <- train1dums[,2:ncol(train1dums)]

#creating function to add all pairwise combinations of variables
LinQuadDat <- function(inpNobs=30994, inpNlinVars=ncol(train1dumsxonly), inpYidx=1:ncol(train1dumsxonly)) {
  # Nobs x Nvars matrix of linear terms:
  xTmp <- train1dumsxonly
  # Make all pairwise products of linear terms,
  # X1*X1, X1*X2, X1*X3, ..., Xn*Xn:
  x2Tmp <- NULL
  tmpCnms <- NULL
  # for each linear term:
  for ( iTmp in 1:ncol(xTmp) ) {
    # multiply it by itself and all other terms,
    # excluding already generated pairwise combinations: 
    for ( jTmp in iTmp:ncol(xTmp) ) {
      x2Tmp <- cbind(x2Tmp,xTmp[,iTmp]*xTmp[,jTmp])
      # maintain vector of column names for quadratic
      # terms along the way:
      tmpCnms <- c(tmpCnms,paste0("X",iTmp,"X",jTmp))
    }
  }
  # name attributes in the matrix of quadratic terms:
  colnames(x2Tmp) <- tmpCnms
  # return data.frame with outcome as a first column,
  # followed by linear, then by quadratic terms:
  data.frame(response=train1dums[,1],xTmp,x2Tmp)
}

#using function to create new data.frame with
#original response variable, all input features
#and their pairwise combinations as multiplicative
#interaction terms
train1dumsints <- LinQuadDat()

#checking new dataset
head(train1dumsints)
dim(train1dumsints)

#rerunning logistic regression model with all predictors
#and their pairwise combinations as interaction terms

lreg2 <- glm(response ~ ., family = binomial(link = "logit"), 
             data = train1dumsints[,c(1:100)])

#printing model and calculating odds ratios 
#and confidence intervals
summary(lreg2)
#exp(lreg2$coefficients)
#exp(confint(lreg2))

#sorting variables by order of importance based on odds ratio
sort(exp(summary(lreg2)$coefficients[,1]), decreasing = TRUE)

#conducting 25-fold cross validation to calculate
#model performance for logistic regression model
data <- train1dumsints[,1:100]
nTries <- 25
lregtrainres2 <- list()
lregtestres2 <- list()
for ( iTry in 1:nTries ) {
  bTrain <- as.numeric(sample(rownames(data),size=nrow(data)*0.8))
    rsTrain <- glm(response~.,family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = data[bTrain,])
      # make and assess predictions in training dataset:
      lregtrain1 <- assess.prediction(data[bTrain,c("response")], ifelse(predict(rsTrain, newdata = data[bTrain,],type = "response") > 0.5,1,0))
      #fit model in test dataset
      rsTest <- glm(response~.,family = binomial(link = "logit"), data = data[-bTrain,])
      # make and assess predictions in test dataset:
      lregtest1 <- assess.prediction(data[-bTrain,c("response")], ifelse(predict(rsTest, newdata = data[-bTrain,], type = "response") > 0.5,1,0))
      #saving results to two separate lists
      lregtrainres2[[iTry]] <- lregtrain1
      lregtestres2[[iTry]] <- lregtest1
  }

#printing results for logistic regression models
#with pairwise interaction terms
#training dataset error
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(lregtrainres2, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(lregtrainres2, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(lregtrainres2, "[[",3))
#all results
lregtrainres2

#test dataset error
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(lregtestres2, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(lregtestres2, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(lregtestres2, "[[",3))
#all results
lregtestres2

```

# Problem 3: linear discriminant analysis (15 points)

Fit linear discriminant analysis model of the outcome `response` as a function of the rest of covariates in the dataset.  Feel free to decide whether you want to use all of them or a subset of those.  Test resulting model performance on multiple splits of the data into training and test subsets, summarize it in terms of accuracy/error/sensitivity/specificity and compare them to those obtained for logistic regression.

Answer: I fit linear discriminant analysis models with all relevant input features from above with k-fold validation and 25 training and testing splits to calculate accuracy (1-accuracy = misclassification error), sensitivity, and specificity for each subset from the resampling procedure. 

These results show that while the training dataset accuracy, sensitivity and specificity were similar for the logistic regression model and the LDA model, the LDA model might be overfit for the test dataset, because the mean sensitivity in the test dataset was considerably lower that in the logistic regression models. 

These results could be related to the linearity (and linear decision boundary) of the LDA model, because the second set of binary logistic regression models above that included interaction terms (and therefore nonlinear relationships), performed far better than the LDA model. Thus, additional modeling approaches that allow for non-linearities in decision boundaries, such as random forest or SVM will also likely have better model performance than the LDA model and logistic regression model with no interaction terms.

```{r Problem 3 Linear Discriminant Analysis}
#conducting 25-fold cross validation to calculate
#model performance for LDA model
data <- train1dums
nTries <- 25
ldatrainres1 <- list()
ldatestres1 <- list()
for ( iTry in 1:nTries ) {
  bTrain <- as.numeric(sample(rownames(data),size=nrow(data)*0.8))
    rsTrain <- lda(response~., data = data[bTrain,])
      # make and assess predictions in training dataset:
      ldatrain1 <- assess.prediction(data[bTrain,c("response")], predict(rsTrain, newdata = data[bTrain,])$class)
      #fit model in test dataset
      rsTest <- lda(response~., data = data[-bTrain,])
      # make and assess predictions in test dataset:
      ldatest1 <- assess.prediction(data[-bTrain,c("response")], predict(rsTest, newdata = data[-bTrain,])$class)
      #saving results to two separate lists
      ldatrainres1[[iTry]] <- ldatrain1
      ldatestres1[[iTry]] <- ldatest1
  }

#printing results from LDA models

#training dataset
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(ldatrainres1, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(ldatrainres1, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(ldatrainres1, "[[",3))
#all results
ldatrainres1

#test dataset
#mean accuracy
```

# Problem 4: random forest (15 points)

Develop random forest model of outcome `response`. Present variable importance plots and comment on relative importance of different attributes in the model.  Did attributes showing up as more important in random forest model also appear as significantly associated with the outcome by logistic regression?  Test model performance on multiple splits of data into training and test subsets, compare test and out-of-bag error estimates, summarize model performance in terms of accuracy/error/sensitivity/specificity and compare to the performance of logistic regression and LDA models above.

Answer: I fit random forest models with all relevant input features from above with k-fold validation and 5 training and testing splits (to keep computing time reasonable) to calculate the out-of-bag error (OOB), accuracy (1-accuracy = misclassification error), sensitivity, and specificity for each subset from the resampling procedure.

The variable importance plots show that "wi_gnq", "zwp_P", "qh", "zwp_Q", and "sb_s2" are the five attributes that have the largest effect on the outcome variable based on the Mean Decrease in Accuracy plot, and "qh", "wi_gnq", "sb_s2", "bw", and "zwp_P" are the five attributes that have the largest effect on the outcome variable based on the Mean Decrease in Gini Coefficient plot. The results for the Mean Decrease in Gini are likely slightly different because this importance metric is computed for all of the trees included in the random forest, yet for the Mean Decrease in Accuracy, these computations are completed for the two classes of the outcome variable across the decision trees in the model.

Importantly, attributes that had significant effects in the logistic regression models also had similarly high importance in the random forest variable importance plots. This suggests that these variables have a significant and moderately strong relationship with the outcome variable and might reveal insights into these variables if the purpose of the analysis is inference (i.e., confirmatory hypothesis testing) or developing understanding about variable inter-relationships.

Compared to the logistic regression models and LDA models above, the random forest performed better in all categories (i.e., accuracy, misclassification error, sensitivity and specificity), and the out-of-bag error was very similar to the test dataset error, as expected.


# Problem 5: SVM (20 points)

Develop SVM model of categorical outcome `response` deciding on the choice of kernel, cost, etc. that appear to yield better performance.  Test model performance on multiple splits of data into training and test subsets, summarize model performance in terms of accuracy/error/sensitivity/specificity and compare to the performance of the rest of the models developed above (logistic regression, LDA, random forest).

Answer: First, I tuned RBF and Polynomial SVM models by testing values of cost, gamma, coef0 (for Polynomial only) and degree (for Polynomial only) to select the values that minimized the error rate and thus increase model performance metrics. The optimal parameters after tuning were cost = 1, gamma = 0.1, coef0 = 1, and degree = 2, which I used in both models in the following steps with k-fold cross-validation resampling.

Next, I fit separate RBF SVM and Polynomial SVM models with all relevant input features from above with k-fold validation and 10 training and testing splits (to keep computing time reasonable) to calculate accuracy (1-accuracy = misclassification error), sensitivity, and specificity for each subset from the resampling procedure.

Compared to the logistic regression and LDA model, both SVM models performed substantially better on all three metrics, whereas the SVM models both performed similar to the random forest model, yet the RBF model's sensitivity was considerably higher than the random forest model. 

These high levels of predictive performance for both the training and test datasets suggest that the non-linear decision boundary allowed by random forests and SVM models, coupled with their lower tendency to overfit, might result in better performance for binary classification. These model also have more tuning parameters, which allow for more adjustments to enhance model performance.

## Problem 6a: compare logistic regression, LDA, random forest and SVM model performance (3 points)

Compare performance of the models developed above (logistic regression, LDA, random forest, SVM) in terms of their accuracy, error and sensitivity/specificity.  Comment on differences and similarities between them.

Comparing all models fit (i.e., logistic regression, LDA, random forest, and the two SVMs with different kernels), the SVM and random forest models consistently perform better, as shown by their mean accuracy, sensitivity and specificity in the plots below.

Importantly, the plot showing box plots of the accuracy for each model type illustrate the importance of using k-fold validation, because the variation in model performance metrics is considerable (i.e., +/- 2 percentage points), which can make a large difference if one were to conduct a single model (i.e., k-fold validation with k = 1 for only 1 training and test dataset split). 

As discussed in the previous problem, these classifiers are likely better prediction generators because they: 1) allow for non-linear decision boundaries, 2) have many parameters that can be tuned to enhance model performance, 3) utilize boosting and bagging to further increase performance metrics, and 4) have safeguards in place to prevent overfitting, which are more limited in logistic regression and LDA models.

# Extra 5 points: KNN model

Develop KNN classifiers for various values of $K$ and compare their performance to that from the rest of the models evaluated herein.  The challenges associated with this task include: a) handling the increase in computational demands of KNN models with the increase in the size of the data, and b) deciding on the choice of the distance that is suitable for a dataset with categorical attributes.

Answer: First, scaled my data to have mean = 0 and SD = 1, and then I tuned my KNN model by using the tune.knn() wrapper function with k = 1 to 50 and examined the plot of the training error and the value for k. This process yielded a value of k = 15 as the optimal value for k, as this value for k had the lowest training dataset error. Models with k > 15 had steadily increasing error, representing increasing bias and potential overfit.

Next, I fit KNN models with all relevant input features from above with k-fold validation and 10 training and testing splits (to keep computing time reasonable) to calculate accuracy (1-accuracy = misclassification error), sensitivity, and specificity for each subset from the resampling procedure. I used the default Euclidean distance in my model and it converged without issues, yet if I did encounter issues (or if I was working with an even higher dimensional dataset), I might experiment with other types of distance metrics including Manhattan distance, Minkowski distance, and even Hassanat or correlational distance (although the latter 2 options would likely increase computation time considerably).

Compared to all models fit above, the KNN model performed similarly to the Polynomial SVM and random forest model in accuracy, similarly to the Polynomial SVM and random forest in sensitivity, and similar to all models in specificity. These results suggest to me that all of these classifiers do a good job in this particular dataset in predicting true negatives, yet the SVM models (especially the RBF SVM), random forest model and KNN model did a better job in predicting true positives, effectively increasing the overall model accuracy.

```{r Extra Points KNN Model}
#scaling dataset to run KNN model
train2 <- train1dums
train2[,2:ncol(train1dums)] <- scale(train1dums[,2:ncol(train1dums)], 
                                     center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

#developing KNN classifier with various
#values of K

#using tine.knn to identify optimal number of neighbors with k = 1 to 30
#with k-fold validation and 10 training and testing datasets due to
#computational time complexity for knn 
set.seed(555)
trainSamp <- as.numeric(sample(rownames(train2),size=nrow(train2)*0.1))

knn1 <- tune.knn(x = train2[trainSamp,2:30], 
                 y = as.factor(train2[trainSamp,c("response")]), 
                 k = c(1,2,3,4,5,10,15,20,30,50),
                 tunecontrol=tune.control(sampling = "cross"), cross=10)

#summarizing knn models with 25 values for k
#and plotting error
summary(knn1)

#best performing model by value for k
knn1$best.model$k
plot(knn1,main = "KNN with k = 1 to k = 50 and Error Rate")

#assessing predictions with k-fold validation and
#10 training and testing splits
data1 <- train2[trainSamp,]
nTries <- 10
knntestres1 <- list()

for ( iTry in 1:nTries ) {
  bTrain <- sample(rownames(data1),size=nrow(data1)*0.8)
    rsTrain <- knn(train = data1[bTrain,1:30], 
                 test = data1[-as.numeric(bTrain),1:30],
                 cl = as.factor(data1[bTrain,c("response")]),
                 k = 15)
      # make and assess predictions in test dataset:
      knntest1 <- assess.prediction(data1[-as.numeric(bTrain),1:30], rsTrain)
      #saving results to a list
      knntestres1[[iTry]] <- knntest1
  rm(rsTrain)
      
      }

#Results for accuracy, sensitivity and specificity for 
#KNN models with k-fold cross-validation and k = 15
#test dataset results
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(knntestres1, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(knntestres1, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(knntestres1, "[[",3))
#all results
knntestres1
```

# Extra 10 points: neural network model

Experiment with fitting neural network models of categorical outcome `response` for this data and evaluate their performance on different splits of the data into training and test. Compare model performance to that for the rest of classifiers developed above.

Answer: First, I tuned my neural network by experimenting with different numbers of hidden nodes and threshold values, to first allow the model to actually converge and second to identify the values that resulted in the optimal model performance. More hidden nodes that 3 and small values for threshold prevented the model from converging in a reasonable period of time or from converging at all, so I tested smaller values for the number of hidden nodes and slightly larger values for the threshold to allow the model to stop iterating when error is slightly higher.

Next, I fit neural network models with all relevant input features from above with k-fold validation and 5 training and testing splits (to keep computing time reasonable) to calculate accuracy (1-accuracy = misclassification error), sensitivity, and specificity for each subset from the resampling procedure.

These results show that the neural net model with 3 hidden nodes performed very similar to the SVM with radial basis kernel in its accuracy, sensitivity and specificity, yet that the computational time was considerably longer for the SVM models, which is likely due to model fitting algorithm complexity (e.g., fitting support vectors takes longer with these data than adjusting weights and forward and backward propagation in the neural net). 

The neural net also performed similarly to the Polynomial SVM and the random forest model, which again, is not particularly surprising because these models allow for a non-linear decision boundary in hyperplane space, so can do better in estimating complex variable relationships and are less impacted by noise variables as compared to LDA or logistic regression. 

```{r Extra 10 points Neural Network Model}
#setting seed for reproducibility
set.seed(555)

#sampling data prior to running neural net models
data1 <- train2[trainSamp,]

nn1 <- neuralnet(response~.,data = data1, hidden=1, linear.output = FALSE, threshold = 0.10, lifesign = "minimal")
nn3 <- neuralnet(response~.,data = data1, hidden=3, linear.output = FALSE, threshold = 0.10, lifesign = "minimal")

#plotting neural net results
#1 hidden node
plot(nn1)
#3 hidden nodes
plot(nn3)

#calculating error for training dataset from model results
errdf <- data.frame(nodes = c(1,3), err = (c(rep(NA),2)))

errdf[1,2] <- sum(nn1$err.fct(nn1$net.result[[1]][,1],nn1$response))
errdf[2,2] <- sum(nn3$err.fct(nn3$net.result[[1]][,1],nn3$response))

#printing training error for both models
errdf

#calculating training and test dataset accuracy with k-fold validation
data1 <- train1dums[sample(rownames(train1dums),size=nrow(train1dums)*0.1),]
nTries <- 5
nnettrainerr1 <- list()
nnettrainres1 <- list()
nnettestres1 <- list()
for ( iTry in 1:nTries ) {
  bTrain <- sample(rownames(data1),size=nrow(data1)*0.8)
    rsTrain <- neuralnet(response~.,data = data1, hidden=3, linear.output = FALSE, threshold = 0.10, lifesign = "minimal")
      # make and assess predictions in training dataset:
      nnettrain1 <- assess.prediction(data1[bTrain,c("response")], ifelse(predict(rsTrain, newdata = data1[bTrain,]) >=0.5,1,0))
      # make and assess predictions in test dataset:
      nnettest1 <- assess.prediction(data1[-as.numeric(bTrain),c("response")], ifelse(predict(rsTrain, newdata = data1[-c(as.numeric(bTrain)),]) >=0.5,1,0))
      #saving results to two separate lists
      nnettrainerr1[[iTry]] <- sum(nn1$err.fct(rsTrain$net.result[[1]][,1],rsTrain$response))
      nnettrainres1[[iTry]] <- nnettrain1
      nnettestres1[[iTry]] <- nnettest1
  rm(rsTrain)
      
      }

#printing training error, training accuracy and test accuracy
#training dataset error
#mean error for training dataset
lapply(nnettrainerr1, mean)
#all results
nnettrainerr1

#training dataset results
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(nnettrainres1, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(nnettrainres1, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(nnettrainres1, "[[",3))
#all results
nnettrainres1

#test dataset results
#mean accuracy
mean(sapply(nnettestres1, "[[",1))
#mean sensitivity
mean(sapply(nnettestres1, "[[",2))
#mean specificity
mean(sapply(nnettestres1, "[[",3))
#all results
nnettestres1
```

# An afterword on the computational demands of the final exam

Because during previous offerings of this course there were always several posts on piazza regarding how long it takes to fit various classifiers to the final exam dataset we have added this note here.

First of all, we most definitely do *not* expect you to *have* to buy capacity from AWS to complete this assignment. You certainly can if you want to, but this course is not about that and this dataset is really not *that* big to require it. Something reasonable/useful can be accomplished for this data with middle of the road hardware. For instance, knitting of the entire official solution for the final exam on 8Gb RAM machine with two i5-7200u cores takes about an hour using single-threaded R/Rstudio and this includes both extra points problems as well as various assessments of the performance of different models as function of data size and so on.

Second, your solution should not take hours and hours to compile. If it does, it could be that it is attempting to do too much, or something is implemented inefficiently, or just plain incorrectly - it is impossible for us to comment on this until we see the code when we grade it. In general, it is often very prudent to "start small" -- fit your model on a random subset of data small enough for the model fitting call to return immediately, check how model performance (both in terms of error and time it takes to compute) scales with the size of the data you are training it on (as you increase it in size, say, two-fold several times), for tuning start with very coarse grid of parameter values and given those results decide what it right for you, etc.

Lastly, making the decision about what is right for the problem at hand, how much is enough, etc. is inherent in this line of work. If you choose to conduct model tuning on a subset of the data - especially if you have some assessment of how the choice of tuning parameter and test error is affected by the size of training dataset - it could be a very wise choice.  If it is more efficient for you to knit each problem separately, by all means feel free to do that - just remember to submit each .Rmd and HTML file that comprises your entire solution. On that note, if you end up using any of the unorthodox setups for your calculations (e.g. AWS, parallel processing, multiple machines, etc. - none of which are essential for solving it correctly) please be sure that when we grade we have every relevant piece of code available - we won't be able to grade your work if we are not clear about how the results were obtained.

In the end, the final exam asks you to assess performance of several classification technologies on a new dataset, decide on which classifier is the best and use it to make predictions for the test data. It is very much up to you how exactly you want to go about it.  There could be many versions of correct and informative solution for that (as there could be just as many if not more that are completely wrong).

As always, best of luck - we are practically done here!

Thanks so much for an amazing and extremely informative semester! :)
